\section[contemnō, contemnere]{contemnō, contemnere — to despise, scorn}

\label{lesson:LA-C514-contemno}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: say the Latin for it shames, then the Latin for shyness.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: contemnō, contemnere}
\textbf{contemnō, contemnere} — \textquotedblleft{}to despise, scorn\textquotedblright{}.

\begin{quote}
Sapiēns pecūniam contemnit.
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
\emph{The wise man despises money.}
\end{quote}

\emph{contemnō, contemnere, contempsī, contemptum}, with the accusative. English \emph{contempt}.

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{contemnō} is built on \emph{con-} and \emph{temnō} \textquotedblleft{}to scorn\textquotedblright{} (Lewis \& Short; EtymDB). English \emph{contempt} and \emph{contemptible} come from it.
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
One more word for telling, explaining and describing at B1.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Say it:} \emph{contemnō, contemnere}
  \item \emph{Say it:} \emph{contemnō, contemnere}, once more
  \item \emph{Say it:} a sentence of your own with \emph{contemnō, contemnere}
  \item \emph{Recall:} say the Latin for it shames, then the Latin for shyness, then say \emph{contemnō, contemnere} again
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What does contemnō, contemnere mean? (\textquotedblleft{}To despise, scorn\textquotedblright{}.) Say it once more.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[spernō, spernere]{spernō, spernere — to reject, spurn}

\label{lesson:LA-C514-sperno}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: say the Latin for shyness, then the Latin for to despise.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: spernō, spernere}
\textbf{spernō, spernere} — \textquotedblleft{}to reject, spurn\textquotedblright{}.

\begin{quote}
Puella amōrem iuvenis spernit.
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
\emph{The girl rejects the young man's love.}
\end{quote}

\emph{spernō, spernere, sprēvī, sprētum}. Stronger than \emph{contemnō}: to push away.

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{spernō} is inherited from a Proto-Indo-European root \emph{sper-} (EtymDB), and English \emph{spurn} is a cousin from the same root (EtymDB).
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
One more word for telling, explaining and describing at B1.
\end{grammarlens}

  \item \emph{Say it:} \emph{spernō, spernere}, once more
  \item \emph{Say it:} a sentence of your own with \emph{spernō, spernere}
  \item \emph{Recall:} say the Latin for shyness, then the Latin for to despise, then say \emph{spernō, spernere} again
\end{itemize}

\section[dēspiciō, dēspicere]{dēspiciō, dēspicere — to look down on, despise}

\label{lesson:LA-C514-despicio}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: say the Latin for to despise, then the Latin for to reject.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: dēspiciō, dēspicere}
\textbf{dēspiciō, dēspicere} — \textquotedblleft{}to look down on, despise\textquotedblright{}.

\begin{quote}
Dīves pauperēs dēspicit.
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
\emph{The rich man looks down on the poor.}
\end{quote}

\emph{dēspiciō, dēspicere, dēspexī, dēspectum}: \emph{dē} 'down' + \emph{speciō} 'to look'. English \emph{despise}.

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{dēspiciō} is built on \emph{dē-} \textquotedblleft{}down\textquotedblright{} and \emph{speciō} \textquotedblleft{}to behold\textquotedblright{} (Lewis \& Short; EtymDB). English \emph{despise} comes from it through Old French.
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
One more word for telling, explaining and describing at B1.
\end{grammarlens}

  \item \emph{Say it:} \emph{dēspiciō, dēspicere}, once more
  \item \emph{Say it:} a sentence of your own with \emph{dēspiciō, dēspicere}
  \item \emph{Recall:} say the Latin for to despise, then the Latin for to reject, then say \emph{dēspiciō, dēspicere} again
\end{itemize}

\section[indignātiō, indignātiōnis]{indignātiō, indignātiōnis — indignation, outrage}

\label{lesson:LA-C514-indignatio}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: say the Latin for to reject, then the Latin for to look down on.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: indignātiō, indignātiōnis}
\textbf{indignātiō, indignātiōnis} — \textquotedblleft{}indignation, outrage\textquotedblright{}.

\begin{quote}
Cīvēs magnā cum indignātiōne clāmant.
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
\emph{The citizens shout with great indignation.}
\end{quote}

Feminine, third declension, from \emph{indignor}. English \emph{indignation}.

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{indignātiō} is the action noun of \emph{indignor} \textquotedblleft{}to be indignant\textquotedblright{} (Lewis \& Short; EtymDB). English \emph{indignation} comes from it.
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
One more word for telling, explaining and describing at B1.
\end{grammarlens}

  \item \emph{Recall:} say the Latin for to reject, then the Latin for to look down on, then say \emph{indignātiō, indignātiōnis} again

\section[displiceō, displicēre]{displiceō, displicēre — to displease}

\label{lesson:LA-C514-displiceo}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: say the Latin for to look down on, then the Latin for indignation.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: displiceō, displicēre}
\textbf{displiceō, displicēre} — \textquotedblleft{}to displease\textquotedblright{}.

\begin{quote}
Haec verba mihi valdē displicent.
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
\emph{These words displease me greatly.}
\end{quote}

\emph{displiceō, displicēre, displicuī, displicitum}, with the dative; the opposite of \emph{placeō}. English \emph{displease}.

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{displiceō} is built on \emph{dis-} \textquotedblleft{}apart, not\textquotedblright{} and \emph{placeō} \textquotedblleft{}to please\textquotedblright{} (Lewis \& Short; EtymDB). English \emph{displease} comes from it through Old French.
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
One more word for telling, explaining and describing at B1.
\end{grammarlens}
